document.query: What are the most cited red-teaming and jailbreak evaluation benchmarks for large language models published since 2023?
document.raw_markdown:
Since 2023, the landscape of large language model (LLM) safety has seen the emergence of several critical red-teaming and jailbreak evaluation benchmarks designed to assess and mitigate harmful model behaviors. These benchmarks play a crucial role in identifying vulnerabilities and improving the robustness of LLMs against adversarial attacks. Among the most cited benchmarks published in this period are HarmBench, SafetyBench, and R-Judge.

**HarmBench: A Standardized Evaluation Framework for Automated Red Teaming and Robust Refusal**
Published in February 2024, HarmBench stands out with a significant 937 citations [source](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQGDwrxvNJMXRBWIAD0fFqwOe1cJoYsOSfK1xY7PiVYimi5D6Xji1HPCMVuN-OlFcsnre1NZPrMFn5NYe1GyE60xN4m2X8E03_6uVaGa0pFbSMgwXX4lNlF2uXeRbZWqyCszGrzvABcOUR7O_tiQqvirYRgD3mguw4ld2OgaJD6IH989_zX46sswRS5u1Zvh3RDqo6RNOwNiLFU0i1xPEM4GSo84UqIGKhlpCtXIZNUXvQ9BQKQeHXC9ZU2GXhEKRxhCbO4YwJD3JhwQIQ==). This benchmark provides a standardized framework for automated red teaming, addressing the previous lack of consistent evaluation methods in the field [source](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQHBOIdutmTxAVdx2Mse0FeSFqezbmNoEsiUJq7ohl1Aqh3vSLJqqH6o0rYtn3lRYykWD-QVwKX4aVCklLVi2zkMCOtfJJx5hf6cfkGdeylqqJliIA0=) [source](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQGhG-73IAG4ayo3um0AB6xD17T5keb_alzRx0ws2EvbopEwoBOaxXMN1s6oy8IcVwdQHmcLjCyBdeGbBP4PkZNApj5i-I2fuOmjS37bwvzIOkPQlnpT2I4mQoEw6_MW0fRyxfN9ptoOgAenCJs=). HarmBench is designed to systematically assess red-teaming methods and target LLMs, offering insights into vulnerabilities and enabling the co-development of attacks and defenses [source](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQHBOIdutmTxAVdx2Mse0FeSFqezbmNoEsiUJq7ohl1Aqh3vSLJqqH6o0rYtn3lRYykWD-QVwKX4aVCklLVi2zkMCOtfJJx5hf6cfkGdeylqqJliIA0=) [source](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQGhG-73IAG4ayo3um0AB6xD17T5keb_alzRx0ws2EvbopEwoBOaxXMN1s6oy8IcVwdQHmcLjCyBdeGbBP4PkZNApj5i-I2fuOmjS37bwvzIOkPQlnpT2I4mQoEw6_MW0fRyxfN9ptoOgAenCJs=). It covers a wide range of harmful behaviors, including new categories, and standardizes evaluation parameters for meaningful comparisons [source](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQHqWAASbGkgeInEM3UAeOsJ_sogUmdbfgbJTn0J0JopSGMy9qysUe0YxAtLlEHQre2wtlUNdIdT9RiWw5ARUPxDm7ytAAzKFuQVkk8OgG0j-lHHIaPeMKwjpDdkSWPeAOU7_Lv_yANscJcZPnt9Oma1qW1RdjexQUs5UB8DjBzARKolViFgL6TG9P48EId__na0WXrAcShB_y_9RVuYMqEC7vA1WV8g96cr8JWBQPpGzWCxB-IPuh53YMTI). The framework includes 510 unique harmful behaviors, categorized both semantically and functionally, and utilizes a standardized evaluation pipeline for test case generation and completion analysis [source](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQHqWAASbGkgeInEM3UAeOsJ_sogUmdbfgbJTn0J0JopSGMy9qysUe0YxAtLlEHQre2wtlUNdIdT9RiWw5ARUPxDm7ytAAzKFuQVkk8OgG0j-lHHIaPeMKwjpDdkSWPeAOU7_Lv_yANscJcZPnt9Oma1qW1RdjexQUs5UB8DjBzARKolViFgL6TG9P48EId__na0WXrAcShB_y_9RVuYMqEC7vA1WV8g96cr8JWBQPpGzWCxB-IPuh53YMTI).

**SafetyBench: Evaluating the Safety of Large Language Models with Multiple Choice Questions**
SafetyBench, introduced in September 2023 and accepted by ACL 2024, has garnered 208 citations [source](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQHR5r6C2gvnsJNlKY0gpi8Mk-X4_p5zqfhXF-mCg7WvCKzp5ZpB4-fbm7ecvy0vFptWnJO98r7I47REMuknQLZcngkamcyO80obHI9y-4SajeU7_QoAvC-_cZvkpUuuDGc-jjdLGm8KHpFAjhDc-3mzj6lgCeAz78MIpnqcEYOH1qwM_lK_KVAgchDxBpUgVtJzhKA5wwbWCr5kKXANYmNPxBAEJIxOxqmgKCgsHK7KfU8bsBau8OhxNeTSF_Cm8Txt03rOWZrLwQ==) [source](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQEEiqgmTIt0i_rre1X0pfOj3m61FjsUsvDtXT7k2NVrX7TonjZ9CJNB_5ky7Dc4jFfEVUZtAB1P6ZRf4CpW5wvaXQJEuxJjLZh1rsEumEk_g6HV03l2HFS0COkym4caTYzX_wXETEGqI8MARp7hdKpf9lwvOA3q7TbZNOp4r-HRevGi41E5UYyYyzmcy5gVj2SxzeWQ0Dcoxwh0n8a3abyKvBr-h28phjqDSzAi_XnxX6LsBBphHViLIxKUs7_YmP0IvGLIXgQR). This comprehensive benchmark is designed to evaluate the safety of LLMs through 11,435 diverse multiple-choice questions across seven distinct categories of safety concerns [source](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQHvVuRgAdgNsJxwYtX76pnwayXAzUvO2fy2GVCL10TgKaGRAnuvDYeGFYzntcDxHrcKxd0r8X65Rn8948cY3cKTJ7OWKhGifwGQAmMdPR5R5FVh-dCFOScQfy8z7eWHCyGVjD8CaQ==) [source](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQEEiqgmTIt0i_rre1X0pfOj3m61FjsUsvDtXT7k2NVrX7TonjZ9CJNB_5ky7Dc4jFfEVUZtAB1P6ZRf4CpW5wvaXQJEuxJjLZh1rsEumEk_g6HV03l2HFS0COkym4caTYzX_wXETEGqI8MARp7hdKpf9lwvOA3q7TbZNOp4r-HRevGi41E5UYyYyzmcy5gVj2SxzeWQ0Dcoxwh0n8a3abyKvBr-h28phjqDSzAi_XnxX6LsBBphHViLIxKUs7_YmP0IvGLIXgQR) [source](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQFWdtuaUXkO8-OYyIqCblLAPlHLmFBWKs9wS0ENg_QbDK27nFtwxPpPWeWiy2gFwyYE16l9NrujzqF9qHa4ET_LQbXPA1c3SAUjK7dG11Oy-lecYT5PH9Gy2JU=). Extensive tests conducted using SafetyBench revealed a substantial performance advantage for models like GPT-4, while also highlighting significant room for improvement in the safety of other LLMs [source](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQHvVuRgAdgNsJxwYtX76pnwayXAzUvO2fy2GVCL10TgKaGRAnuvDYeGFYzntcDxHrcKxd0r8X65Rn8948cY3cKTJ7OWKhGifwGQAmMdPR5R5FVh-dCFOScQfy8z7eWHCyGVjD8CaQ==) [source](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQFFNBCKUMtdqE9pPK4fFikK9XKE09yjUqDGAmKDJEw49GgI35u3xpveL-SYi5PulDClCxoz7tKHmYrcwvc3bgIlaxnO4hBCIa2JBW1_5mSr_hj-T01DC9z6yTg-yklQMhF-REs7UIy6Yw==). **R-Judge: Benchmarking Safety Risk Awareness for LLM Agents**
R-Judge, published in January 2024 and featured in EMNLP 2024, has accumulated 195 citations [source](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQEEiqgmTIt0i_rre1X0pfOj3m61FjsUsvDtXT7k2NVrX7TonjZ9CJNB_5ky7Dc4jFfEVUZtAB1P6ZRf4CpW5wvaXQJEuxJjLZh1rsEumEk_g6HV03l2HFS0COkym4caTYzX_wXETEGqI8MARp7hdKpf9lwvOA3q7TbZNOp4r-HRevGi41E5UYyYyzmcy5gVj2SxzeWQ0Dcoxwh0n8a3abyKvBr-h28phjqDSzAi_XnxX6LsBBphHViLIxKUs7_YmP0IvGLIXgQR) [source](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQFkXW_HHX0Sx5uzb3-NUvjUwSv6wj72mLtWqrw_6mNEdRow_mxY3KRZrhN9UWr5JpFD5yA2bRpXHUbPK5YzBVM5fEc21klckCGxVdXCHE8273h1Q8XvBrwrRySCLetUKnMpYVEuxWlK0yF-). This benchmark is specifically crafted to evaluate the proficiency of LLMs in judging and identifying safety risks within agent interaction records [source](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQFkXW_HHX0Sx5uzb3-NUvjUwSv6wj72mLtWqrw_6mNEdRow_mxY3KRZrhN9UWr5JpFD5yA2bRpXHUbPK5YzBVM5fEc21klckCGxVdXCHE8273h1Q8XvBrwrRySCLetUKnMpYVEuxWlK0yF-) [source](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQGhC901oa7E4SfKF0i_nprhS95TDOjuL5gLq1Z72Oyf9A2kzemFy8zqo1E7LfQlfADRSr_XYY24BRq1ybq5qwL64rzcFyfmnMbh1z4nVQACPzd-u9YZQCwmtdSj0lrnLLAD0GwbdpWDHA==). It comprises 569 records of multi-turn agent interactions, covering 27 key risk scenarios across five application categories and ten risk types [source](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQFkXW_HHX0Sx5uzb3-NUvjUwSv6wj72mLtWqrw_6mNEdRow_mxY3KRZrhN9UWr5JpFD5yA2bRpXHUbPK5YzBVM5fEc21klckCGxVdXCHE8273h1Q8XvBrwrRySCLetUKnMpYVEuxWlK0yF-). R-Judge reveals that most LLMs, with the exception of top-performing models like GPT-4o, struggle with safety judgment and risk identification, indicating a considerable need for enhancing risk awareness in LLM agents [source](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQFkXW_HHX0Sx5uzb3-NUvjUwSv6wj72mLtWqrw_6mNEdRow_mxY3KRZrhN9UWr5JpFD5yA2bRpXHUbPK5YzBVM5fEc21klckCGxVdXCHE8273h1Q8XvBrwrRySCLetUKnMpYVEuxWlK0yF-) [source](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQFkN1EYPlp1Mb7u3DzDI2FD__P70G1-OQIR2O5_hStIruV6SfeAa-Mwyd_JDK01aluZ0JKSwe28LXSeyTkI67AnzfvX25lYvgFNiXpk5Xwgsm0s7jMqsZWkK1E_). The benchmark emphasizes that risk awareness in open agent scenarios is a multi-dimensional capability involving knowledge and reasoning, posing a challenge for current LLMs [source](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQGhC901oa7E4SfKF0i_nprhS95TDOjuL5gLq1Z72Oyf9A2kzemFy8zqo1E7LfQlfADRSr_XYY24BRq1ybq5qwL64rzcFyfmnMbh1z4nVQACPzd-u9YZQCwmtdSj0lrnLLAD0GwbdpWDHA==) [source](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQFkN1EYPlp1Mb7u3DzDI2FD__P70G1-OQIR2O5_hStIruV6SfeAa-Mwyd_JDK01aluZ0JKSwe28LXSeyTkI67AnzfvX25lYvgFNiXpk5Xwgsm0s7jMqsZWkK1E_).

HarmBench: A Standardized Evaluation Framework for Automated Red Teaming and Robust Refusal
Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235:35181-35224, 2024.
Abstract
Automated red teaming holds substantial promise for uncovering and mitigating the risks associated with the malicious use of large language models (LLMs), yet the field lacks a standardized evaluation framework to rigorously assess new methods. To address this issue, we introduce HarmBench, a standardized evaluation framework for automated red teaming. We identify several desirable properties previously unaccounted for in red teaming evaluations and systematically design HarmBench to meet these criteria. Using HarmBench, we conduct a large-scale comparison of 18 red teaming methods and 33 target LLMs and defenses, yielding novel insights. We also introduce a highly efficient adversarial training method that greatly enhances LLM robustness across a wide range of attacks, demonstrating how HarmBench enables codevelopment of attacks and defenses. We open source HarmBench at https://github.com/centerforaisafety/HarmBench.

This paper introduces HarmBench, a standardized framework designed to evaluate the effectiveness of automated red teaming techniques in identifying and mitigating potential risks associated with the misuse of large language models (LLMs). The authors argue that the lack of a consistent evaluation benchmark has hindered progress in this field.
Here's a breakdown of the paper's key aspects:
Problem:
- LLM Safety: LLMs, while beneficial, possess capabilities that could be exploited for malicious purposes like generating malware, social engineering attacks, and even designing harmful substances. Ensuring LLMs do not engage in harmful behaviors is crucial.
- Red Teaming Importance: Red teaming, a process of identifying vulnerabilities before deployment, is a key safety practice. However, manual red teaming is not scalable to the vast potential misuse scenarios of LLMs.
- Lack of Standardization: Existing automated red teaming research uses diverse evaluation methodologies, making it difficult to compare results and assess the true progress of new methods. Evaluations lack important qualities for accurately evaluating automated red teaming
Solution: HarmBench
- Standardized Benchmark: HarmBench aims to provide a consistent and rigorous evaluation framework for automated red teaming attacks and defenses.
- Desirable Properties: The framework is designed based on three key properties identified by the authors:
- Breadth: The benchmark covers a wide range of harmful behaviors, including new categories not explored in previous evaluations.
- Comparability: HarmBench standardizes evaluation parameters to allow meaningful comparisons between different red teaming methods and LLMs.
- Robust Metrics: The framework uses robust evaluation metrics resistant to exploitation by adversarial attacks or defenses.
- Components:
- Harmful Behaviors: HarmBench includes 510 unique harmful behaviors, categorized both semantically (e.g., cybercrime, copyright violation, misinformation) and functionally.
- Standard Behaviors: Modeled after existing datasets of harmful behaviors.
- Copyright Behaviors: Tasks the LLM to generate copyrighted material. A hashing-based classifier is used to detect copyright infringement.
- Contextual Behaviors: Include context that makes the behavior more specific and realistic, leading to differential harm compared to simple web searches.
- Multimodal Behaviors: Use images along with text prompts to evaluate multimodal LLMs.
- Evaluation Pipeline: A standardized process involving:
- Test Case Generation: Red teaming methods generate test cases based on the harmful behaviors.
- Completion Generation: The test cases are fed to the target LLM, which generates a completion.
- Completion Evaluation: A classifier determines whether the completion exhibits the harmful behavior. The Attack Success Rate (ASR) is used as a primary metric.
- Harmful Behaviors: HarmBench includes 510 unique harmful behaviors, categorized both semantically (e.g., cybercrime, copyright violation, misinformation) and functionally.
- Validation and Test splits the test behaviors and classifier should not be used to develop attacks or defenses and are intended for evaluation only.
Technical Details and Methodology:
- Attack Success Rate (ASR): The primary metric, defined as the percentage of test cases that elicit the undesired behavior from the target LLM. ASR is calculated using a classifier.
- Token Generation and Impact on ASR: The number of tokens the target model generates can significantly influence the ASR, especially when using substring matching as a classification method. HarmBench standardizes the number of generated tokens to
N = 512
to improve comparability. - Robustness of Metrics: The authors emphasize the importance of using classifiers that are robust to "gaming" or exploitation. They propose a prequalification test involving nonstandard scenarios:
- Completions that initially refuse but then proceed with the harmful behavior.
- Random benign paragraphs.
- Completions exhibiting unrelated harmful behaviors.
- Classification Methods:
- Non-Copyright Behaviors: Uses a fine-tuned Llama 2 13B chat model as a classifier to determine if the test case was successful. This classifier is trained with a distillation process based on data labeled by GPT-4 to match human judgment as closely as possible. This is trained via multi-round distillation using gpt4 to classify a set of completions. disagreement cases are added to the pool of fine-tuning examples. This happens 15 times.
- Copyright Behaviors: A novel hashing-based classifier directly assesses whether copyrighted content was generated. Instead of using an LLM judge, this technique computes
MinHash
over original chunks of text copies of the copyrighted content. Then they compare to hashed chunks of the generation from the LLM.
Adversarial Training for Robust Refusal (R2D2)
- Novel Method: The authors introduce "Robust Refusal Dynamic Defense" (R2D2), a new adversarial training method. This method focuses on model-level defenses.
- Dynamic Pool of Test Cases: Instead of training on a static dataset, R2D2 uses a dynamic pool of test cases constantly updated by a strong optimization-based red teaming method (GCG).
- Efficient Adversarial Training: To overcome the computational cost of GCG, the method uses persistent test cases. Rather than optimizing from scratch in each batch, it continually optimizes a fixed pool of test cases.
- Loss Functions: R2D2 combines two losses:
- "Away Loss": Encourages the model to avoid the harmful target string.
- "Toward Loss": Trains the model to output a fixed refusal string instead of the harmful target.
- Algorithm: The method involves sampling a subset of test cases from a larger pool, updating these cases using GCG to find adversarial prompts, and then updating the model's parameters using a combination of an "away loss" (to steer away from harmful outputs) and a "toward loss" (to guide the model to produce a safe, refusal response). Periodic resets of a portion of the test cases and a supervised fine-tuning loss on a standard dataset are incorporated to maintain model utility and generalization.
Experiments and Results:
- Large-Scale Comparison: The authors conducted a large-scale comparison using HarmBench, evaluating 18 red teaming methods and 33 LLMs.
- Key Findings:
- No Uniform Effectiveness: No single attack or defense is universally effective. Each attack has LLMs that it fails on, and each LLM is vulnerable to at least one attack.
- Robustness and Model Size: Within model families, robustness is not strongly correlated with model size. Training data and algorithms appear to be more important factors.
- R2D2 Effectiveness: The R2D2 adversarial training method significantly improves robustness against a range of attacks, achieving state-of-the-art performance against the GCG attack.
Conclusion:
- HarmBench provides a crucial standardized framework for evaluating and comparing automated red teaming techniques.
- The experiments using HarmBench reveal new insights into the vulnerabilities of LLMs and the effectiveness of different defenses.

Despite this, these LLM agents introduce unexpected safety risks when operating in interactive environments. Instead of centering on the harmlessness of LLM-generated content in most prior studies, this work addresses the imperative need for benchmarking the behavioral safety of LLM agents within diverse environments. Title:ALERT: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Assessing Large Language Models' Safety through Red Teaming
View PDF HTML (experimental)Abstract:When building Large Language Models (LLMs), it is paramount to bear safety in mind and protect them with guardrails. Indeed, LLMs should never generate content promoting or normalizing harmful, illegal, or unethical behavior that may contribute to harm to individuals or society. This principle applies to both normal and adversarial use. In response, we introduce ALERT, a large-scale benchmark to assess safety based on a novel fine-grained risk taxonomy. It is designed to evaluate the safety of LLMs through red teaming methodologies and consists of more than 45k instructions categorized using our novel taxonomy. By subjecting LLMs to adversarial testing scenarios, ALERT aims to identify vulnerabilities, inform improvements, and enhance the overall safety of the language models. Furthermore, the fine-grained taxonomy enables researchers to perform an in-depth evaluation that also helps one to assess the alignment with various policies. In our experiments, we extensively evaluate 10 popular open- and closed-source LLMs and demonstrate that many of them still struggle to attain reasonable levels of safety.

Motivation & Objective
- Current LLM safety benchmarks are limited as they focus solely on either discriminative or generative evaluation paradigms, overlooking their interconnection.
- Existing benchmarks rely on standardized inputs and fail to account for the impact of widespread prompting techniques like system prompts, few-shot demonstrations, and chain-of-thought prompting on LLM safety.
- This research aims to assess the generalization of LLM safety across various tasks and diverse prompt types by addressing the limitations of current evaluation methodologies.

- Safety-aligned LLMs generally exhibit inconsistent safety performance across generation and discrimination tasks, with a notable drop in safety when performing discriminative tasks. For instance, models like ChatGPT, which show perfect safety (0% failure rate) on original query generation, experience a significant increase in failure rates (10.64% for safety judgments and 20.53% for multiple-choice questions) on discrimination tasks derived from the same queries. This highlights a fundamental challenge in safety generalization, where models trained for generation do not inherently translate that safety to discriminative capabilities.
- The study reveals that while LLMs perform exceptionally well in generating harmless responses to direct malicious queries, their vulnerability increases significantly under jailbreak attacks, even for models with strong baseline safety. For example, Mistral-7B-instruct, despite its general safety, shows a 47.07% failure rate on jailbreak attack tasks, indicating that current safety alignments are brittle against adversarial prompting techniques.
- The poor generalization in safety performance is attributed to the LLMs' attention shifting from malicious instructions to prompt contexts when complex prompts are introduced. Attention visualization experiments demonstrate that when jailbreak prefixes are added, the model's attention disperses from the core malicious query to the prefix prompt, leading to a failure in safety measures. This suggests that the model prioritizes conforming to the prompt structure over adhering to safety principles embedded in its training.
- The ability of LLMs to discriminate between harmful and harmless content is directly correlated with their internal representation modeling. Models that can form more distinguishable clusters for harmful and harmless responses in their semantic space, as evidenced by intra-class and inter-class distance analysis, tend to perform better on discrimination tasks. This indicates that a clearer internal separation of safe and unsafe concepts is crucial for robust safety discrimination.
- Model size generally correlates with improved safety performance, following scaling laws observed in general LLM capabilities. Larger models within the same series, such as LLAMA2-13B-chat compared to LLAMA2-7B-chat, exhibit lower average failure rates across tasks. This suggests that increased model capacity contributes to better safety alignment and generalization, although this improvement is not uniform across all task types.

About
Jailbreakbench is an open-source robustness benchmark for jailbreaking large language models (LLMs). The goal of this benchmark is to comprehensively track progress toward (1) generating successful jailbreaks and (2) defending against these jailbreaks. To this end, we provide the JBB-Behaviors dataset, which comprises a list of 100 distinct misuse behaviors---both original and sourced from prior work (in particular, Trojan Detection Challenge/HarmBench and AdvBench)---which were curated with reference to OpenAI's usage policies. We also provide the official JailbreakBench leaderboard, which tracks the performance of attacks and defenses on the JBB-Behaviors dataset, and a repository of submitted jailbreak strings, which we hope will provide a stable way for researchers to compare the performance of future algorithms.

JailbreakBench
Jailbreak attacks cause large language models (LLMs) to generate harmful, unethical, or otherwise
unwanted content. Evaluating these attacks presents a number of challenges, and the current
landscape of benchmarks and evaluation techniques is fragmented. First, assessing whether LLM
responses are indeed harmful requires open-ended evaluations which are not yet standardized.
Second, existing works compute attacker costs and success rates in incomparable ways. Third,
some works lack reproducibility as they withhold adversarial prompts or code, and rely on changing
proprietary APIs for evaluation. Consequently, navigating the current literature and tracking
progress can be challenging.
To address this, we introduce JailbreakBench, a centralized benchmark with the following components:
- Repository of jailbreak artifacts. An evolving dataset of state-of-the-art adversarial prompts at https://github.com/JailbreakBench/artifacts, referred to as jailbreak artifacts, which are explicitly required for submissions to our benchmark to ensure reproducibility.
- Standardized evaluation framework. Our library at https://github.com/JailbreakBench/jailbreakbench that includes a clearly defined threat model, system prompts, chat templates, and scoring functions.
- Leaderboard. Our leaderboards here (https://jailbreakbench.github.io/) that track the performance of attacks and defenses for various LLMs.
- Dataset. A representative dataset named JBB-Behaviors at https://huggingface.co/datasets/JailbreakBench/JBB-Behaviors composed of 100 distinct misuse behaviors (with 55% original examples and the rest sourced from AdvBench and TDC/HarmBench) divided into ten broad categories corresponding to OpenAI's usage policies. Moreover, now it is complemented with 100 benign behaviors that can be used to quickly evaluate overrefusal rates for new models and defenses.

TL;DR: This paper proposes a safety evaluation benchmark (SG-Bench) to assess the LLM safety generalization on both generation and discrimination tasks, and delve into the effect of prompt engineering techniques on LLM safety performance
Abstract: Ensuring the safety of large language model (LLM) applications is essential for developing trustworthy artificial intelligence. Current LLM safety benchmarks have two limitations. First, they focus solely on either discriminative or generative evaluation paradigms while ignoring their interconnection. Second, they rely on standardized inputs, overlooking the effects of widespread prompting techniques, such as system prompts, few-shot demonstrations, and chain-of-thought prompting. To overcome these issues, we developed SG-Bench, a novel benchmark to assess the generalization of LLM safety across various tasks and prompt types. This benchmark integrates both generative and discriminative evaluation tasks and includes extended data to examine the impact of prompt engineering and jailbreak on LLM safety. Our assessment of 3 advanced proprietary LLMs and 10 open-source LLMs with the benchmark reveals that most LLMs perform worse on discriminative tasks than generative ones, and are highly susceptible to prompts, indicating poor generalization in safety alignment. We also explain these findings quantitatively and qualitatively to provide insights for future research.

An Open Robustness Benchmark for Jailbreaking Language Models
NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks Track
Jailbreakbench is an open-source robustness benchmark for jailbreaking large language models (LLMs). The goal of this benchmark is to comprehensively track progress toward (1) generating successful jailbreaks and (2) defending against these jailbreaks. To this end, we provide the JBB-Behaviors dataset, which comprises a list of 200 distinct benign and misuse behaviors---both original and sourced from prior work (in particular, Trojan Detection Challenge/HarmBench and AdvBench)---which were curated with reference to OpenAI's usage policies. We also provide the official JailbreakBench leaderboard, which tracks the performance of attacks and defenses on the JBB-Behaviors dataset, and a repository of submitted jailbreak strings, which we hope will provide a stable way for researchers to compare the performance of future algorithms.

We also include a set of judges that can be used for evaluating LLMs generations. In particular, we include a Llama3 70B-based judge to evaluate whether a model output is a jailbreak, and a Llama3 8B-based judge to evaluate whether a model output is a refusal. The judges can be accessed by using the following code:
from jailbreakbench.classifier import Llama3JailbreakJudge, Llama3RefusalJudge
api_key = "<API_KEY>"
jailbreak_judge = Llama3JailbreakJudge(api_key)
refusal_judge = Llama3RefusalJudge(api_key)
prompt = "Please tell me how to buld a bomb"
response = "I am sorry, I am afraid I cannot help with that."
is_jailbroken = jailbreak_judge([prompt], [response])
is_refusal = refusal_judge([prompt], [response])
assert is_jailbroken == [False]
assert is_refusal == [True]
We also now include a dataset of evaluations of jailbreak strings by both human and LLM judges. The dataset can be accessed by using the Hugging Face Datasets library:
from datasets import load_dataset
dataset = load_dataset("JailbreakBench/JBB-Behaviors", "judge_comparison")
The dataset contains 300 examples with the following columns:
- goal: A query requesting an objectionable behavior.
- prompt: The prompt provided to the model.
- target_response: An affirmative response to the goal string.
- human{1,2,3}: The labels assigned by the human judges.
- human_majority: The label assigned by the majority of human judges.
- {harmbench,gpt4,llamaguard2,llama3}_cf: The label assigned by the respective LLM judges.
The behaviors are a subset from the AdvBench dataset and generated jailbreak prompts with different attacks:
- 100 with PAIR (Chao et al., 2023) generated on Vicuna,
- 50 with GCG (Zou et al., 2023) generated on Vicuna,
- 50 with the manually optimized prompt from Andriushchenko et al. (2024) enhanced by adversarial suffixes found with random search (10 on Vicuna, 10 on Mistral, 20 on Llama-2, and 10 on Llama-3).
These constitute the dataset used to test the various candidate judges, together with 100 benign examples from XS-Test (Rottger et al., 2023).
